formNote: The Shuowen: 符，信也。漢制以竹，長六寸，分而相合 — “a token of trust: in Han practice of bamboo, six inches long, split and matched.” Mojidata IDS: ⿱𥫗付.
summary: A tally split in two, whose halves must match: a token of authority, and the word for agreeing (符合). In Daoist practice 符 is the written talisman; in Vietnamese the same word lives on as bùa, a charm.
placement: Low at the centre, set back: the tally, with 印 the seal to its upper right. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus, from general knowledge; not yet checked against B–S 2014.

satellites.title: Split and Matched
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen describes the Han tally: bamboo, six inches long, split, with each party keeping a half (分而相合). Proof was a fit. Modern 符合, “to tally, to accord”, keeps the image.

satellites.title: Daoist Talismans
satellites.evidence: Daoist practice uses 符, talismans in stylised script, to summon, protect and command; 符籙 names the talismans together with the registers of spirits that go with them. The tally that authenticated an official became a writing that authorises.
satellites.caveat: Reported, never prescribed. Drafted by Baracus from general knowledge.
gaps: Register a Daoist primary source (e.g. the Daozang) for 符籙.

satellites.title: A Vietnamese Charm
satellites.evidence: Unihan gives bùa as the Vietnamese reading of 符: the everyday word for an amulet or charm. The tally’s talismanic sense is the one that travelled into ordinary Vietnamese.
satellites.caveat: Baracus adds, from general knowledge, that the Sino-Vietnamese reading proper is phù and that bùa is an older or vernacular layer; that is not in the Unihan citation.
